units.title: Hello, Clojure!
units.summary: Write your first Clojure program, print text with println, calculate in prefix notation and join text with str.

lesson.md: A Clojure program is a list of expressions. An expression in parentheses is a **function call**: the first item is the function, the other items are its arguments. The function `println` prints its arguments and then ends the line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Clojure!"`, is a **string**.
`println` accepts several arguments and puts a space between them. Numbers are written without quotes. Every `println` starts a new line.

In mathematics you write `1 + 2`. In Clojure the operator comes first, like every other function: `(+ 1 2)`. This is called **prefix notation**. The functions `+` (add), `-` (subtract) and `*` (multiply) accept any number of arguments, so `(+ 1 2 3)` is `6`.
You can put expressions inside other expressions. Clojure first calculates the inner ones. There are no precedence rules to remember: the parentheses show the order.
The function `str` joins all its arguments into one string. Unlike `println`, it adds no spaces, so you write them yourself. Numbers become text, too.
Every opening parenthesis `(` needs a closing one `)`. A missing `)` is the most common error for beginners, so count them when your program does not run.

units.title: Values
units.summary: Get to know numbers, ratios, strings, keywords, booleans and nil, and give values a name with def.

lesson.md: Whole numbers like `42` are **integers**. Numbers with a decimal point, like `3.5`, are **decimal numbers**. When a decimal number takes part in a calculation, the result is a decimal number, too.

When you divide two integers with `/` and the result is not whole, Clojure gives a **ratio**: an exact fraction like `7/2`. Nothing is rounded. If you want a decimal result, use a decimal number. `quot` gives the whole part of a division and `mod` gives the rest.
`def` gives a value a name. After `(def age 30)`, the name `age` stands for `30`. Names can contain a dash, like `first-name`, and Clojure programmers write them this way.

lesson.code:
(def price 4)
(def amount 3)
(def total (* price amount))
(println "Total:" total)

lesson.md: A **keyword** is a name that starts with a colon, like `:red`. It stands for itself, and you use it as a label, for example for the keys of a map (you meet maps in a later unit). The **booleans** `true` and `false` are the answers to yes-or-no questions. `nil` means **no value**.

`println` shows a string without quotes. `prn` shows every value the way you write it in code, so strings keep their quotes. This helps you see what a value really is. The function `count` gives the number of characters in a string.
Functions whose names end with `?` answer a yes-or-no question with `true` or `false`. For example, `(string? "hi")` and `(nil? nil)` are both `true`, and `(number? "5")` is `false`.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with defn and fn, use the short form #(...), and accept different numbers of arguments.

lesson.md: `defn` defines a function. After `defn` come the name, the **parameters** in square brackets and the body. A function returns the value of its last expression. Clojure has no `return` keyword.
A function can have several parameters. You call your own functions the same way as the built-in ones.
The body can contain several expressions. All of them run in order, but only the value of the last one is returned.

`fn` creates a function without a name, an **anonymous function**. You can give it a name with `def` or call it directly. The short form `#(...)` is even shorter: inside it, `%` is the argument. With several arguments you write `%1`, `%2` and so on.

The number of arguments a function takes is its **arity**. One function can have several arities. Each version gets its own parentheses with its parameters and body. One version can call another one, for example to fill in a default value.
If you call a function with a number of arguments it does not accept, the program stops with an error that says `Wrong number of args`.
Function names use lowercase words joined with dashes, like `total-price`. Choose names that say what the function returns or does.

card: `(defn square [x] (* x x))` defines a function
The last expression is the return value
`(fn [x] (* 2 x))` is a function without a name
`#(* 2 %)` is the short form, `%1 %2` for more arguments

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Compare values, choose between results with if, when and cond, and combine conditions with and, or and not.

lesson.md: Comparisons are functions, too. `=` checks if values are equal, `not=` checks if they are different, and `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare numbers. They return `true` or `false`. `(< 1 2 3)` checks if the numbers go up from left to right.
`if` takes three parts: a condition, the value when the condition is true, and the value when it is false. `if` is an expression, so it returns a value that you can print or use.
Only `false` and `nil` count as false. Every other value counts as true, even `0` and the empty string `""`.
`when` has only one branch, and it can contain several expressions. They all run when the condition is true. When the condition is false, nothing runs and `when` returns `nil`.

`cond` takes pairs of a test and a result. It returns the result of the first test that is true and ignores the rest. The keyword `:else` as the last test always counts as true, so it catches all other cases.
`and` is true when all its conditions are true. `or` is true when at least one is true. `not` turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.

lesson.code:
(def age 20)
(def member true)
(println (and (>= age 18) member))
(println (or (< age 12) (> age 65)))
(println (not member))

lesson.md: In Clojure, `=` only compares. It never changes a value. You give names to values with `def`.

`(when test ...)` runs several expressions or returns `nil`

units.title: Collections
units.summary: Keep many values in vectors, lists, maps and sets, and read and add elements with get, count and conj.

lesson.md: A **vector** keeps values in order, written in square brackets: `[1 2 3]`. `count` gives the number of elements and `first` the first one. `get` gives the element at an index. The index starts at `0`, and an index that does not exist gives `nil`.
`conj` adds an element. For a vector it adds it at the end. Clojure collections never change: `conj` returns a new vector, and the old one stays the same. This is called **immutability**.
A **list** is written in parentheses. But in code, parentheses mean a function call, so you put a quote `'` in front of a list of data: `'(1 2 3)`. `conj` adds to the front of a list.

A **map** stores pairs of a key and a value in curly braces. The keys are often keywords. `get` looks up the value for a key, and a keyword can also look itself up: `(:age person)`. A missing key gives `nil`, or the default value you pass to `get` as third argument. Commas count as spaces, and Clojure prints them between the pairs.
A **set** contains every value at most once and is written `#{...}`. `contains?` checks if a value is in the set. Adding a value that is already there changes nothing.
Sets and large maps have no fixed order. Do not rely on the order in which their elements are printed.

units.title: Sequences
units.summary: Process collections step by step with map, filter and reduce, create numbers with range, and chain steps with ->>.

lesson.md: `range` creates numbers. `(range 5)` gives the numbers from `0` to `4`, and `(range 1 6)` the numbers from `1` to `5`: the end is not included. A third argument sets the step. The result is a **sequence**, which prints in parentheses like a list.
`map` calls a function on every element and returns a new sequence with the results. The function `inc` adds 1 to a number. You can pass any function to `map`: a built-in one, your own or a `#(...)`.
`filter` keeps the elements for which the function returns true. The functions `even?` and `odd?` check if a number is even or odd.

`reduce` combines all elements into one value with a function of two arguments. `(reduce + [1 2 3 4])` calculates `1 + 2`, then adds `3`, then `4`. You can also pass a start value before the collection.

`take` gives the first elements of a sequence. `(range)` without arguments never ends, but that is no problem: Clojure sequences are **lazy**, which means an element is only calculated when it is needed.
Nested calls are read from the inside out. The macro `->>` lets you write the steps from top to bottom instead: it puts the result of each step as the **last** argument into the next step.
The example above does the same as `(reduce + (map #(* % %) (filter odd? (range 1 11))))`. With `->>` you can read the steps in the order they happen.

units.title: Local names and recursion
units.summary: Give values local names with let, write functions that call themselves, and repeat steps with loop and recur.

lesson.md: `let` gives values names that exist only inside the `let`. First comes a vector with pairs of names and values, then the body. A later name can use the earlier ones. The `let` returns the value of its last expression.

lesson.code:
(defn price-with-tax [price]
  (let [tax (* price 0.25)
        total (+ price tax)]
    (str "Tax: " tax ", total: " total)))

(println (price-with-tax 80))

lesson.md: A name from `let` is not visible outside. Inside the `let`, it hides a name from `def` with the same name, but the `def` value does not change.

lesson.code:
(def x 1)
(let [x 10
      y (* x 2)]
  (println x y))
(println x)

lesson.md: A function can call itself. This is called **recursion**. It needs a **base case**, where it stops calling itself. The function `dec` subtracts 1 from a number. The **factorial** of 5 is 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
Each call waits for the result of the next call. Every waiting call needs memory, so with many thousands of calls the program stops with a `StackOverflowError`.

`loop` sets starting values, like `let`. `recur` jumps back to the start of the `loop` with new values. It needs no extra memory, so it can repeat millions of times. `recur` must be the last step of the loop: nothing may run after it.
A loop often carries a result along, like `total` here. When the loop stops calling `recur`, it returns the value of its last expression.

lesson.code:
(defn sum-to [n]
  (loop [i 1
         total 0]
    (if (> i n)
      total
      (recur (inc i) (+ total i)))))

(println (sum-to 100))

lesson.md: `recur` also works without `loop`: then it jumps back to the start of the function. In everyday code you often use `map`, `filter` and `reduce` instead of writing loops yourself.

card: `(let [a 1 b (+ a 1)] (* a b))` local names
Recursion: a function calls itself and needs a base case

units.title: Working with maps
units.summary: Change maps with assoc, dissoc and update, read keys and values, chain steps with -> and take values out with destructuring.

lesson.md: `assoc` returns a new map with a key added or changed. `dissoc` returns a new map without a key. Like all Clojure collections, the original map never changes.
`update` changes a value with a function. `(update m :k f)` calls `f` with the old value and stores the result. Extra arguments go to the function after the old value.
`keys` gives all keys of a map and `vals` all values. Small maps keep the order in which you wrote them, but in general a map has no fixed order.

The macro `->` works like `->>`, but it puts each result as the **first** argument into the next step. This fits maps well, because `assoc`, `dissoc` and `update` take the map as their first argument.

**Destructuring** takes values out of a collection right where you name them, in a `let` or in the parameters of a function. A vector like `[x y]` takes elements by position. A map like `{:keys [city zip]}` takes the values of the keys `:city` and `:zip`.

lesson.code:
(let [[x y] [3 4]]
  (println (+ x y)))

(defn greet [{:keys [first-name city]}]
  (str first-name " lives in " city))

(println (greet {:first-name "Ada" :city "London"}))

lesson.md: A key that is missing from the map gives `nil` in destructuring. As a rule of thumb, use `->` for maps and `->>` for sequences.
